newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Virtual imagery to revolutionise advertising.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Virtual imagery to revolutionise advertising.

text.p: A new dimension of virtual imagery is set to revolutionise television advertising at major world sports and cultural events, proponents of the technology say.
Using electronically-created images, virtual imaging can make adverts appear floating over a playing field during a high-profile sports event, on the playing field itself, or as billboards around it.
In a recent soccer match in Mexico the technology was used to create a three-dimensional revolving can floating over the field.

Keith Impey, director of the London-based International Sports Group, which is marketing the EPSIS virtual advertising system in Britain, said the technology offers the flexibility to create almost any kind of image.
"The technology will allow you to have a car drive across the pitch," Impey said.
VIRTUAL IMAGES "THE FUTURE OF ADVERTISING"
Impey said it was impossible to estimate the potential size of the virtual advertising market because it is such a new field.
"The market (currently) doesn't exist," Impey said. "But virtual imaging could affect anything anyone sees on a live event...whether it's a live concert or a cultural event or sport."
For Impey the future is clear. "It will be a success," he said. "It is the future of advertising."
The financial rewards are split between the event owners and the advertisers.

"The broadcaster is just the carrier," said Patrick Burton, group media manager for drinks company Allied Domecq. "But if the broadcaster owns the event then you have the possibility of selling the advertising rights to different people in different countries.
"Estimates are you could probably double your advertising revenue from selling international events," Burton said.
SPORTS ADS TO TARGET SPECIFIC MARKETS
Adverts can be changed throughout a sports event and modified for different audiences, allowing viewers in France to see entirely different ads to those in Britain watching the same broadcast.
"The potential is to localise the advertising during sporting events," Kobi Bendel, president of Tel Aviv-based SciDel, told Reuters.
SciDel, a joint venture between Scitex Corp Ltd and Bendel, is marketing the SciTex system around the world and has offices in London and New York, as well as Tel Aviv.
Bendel said SciDel has invested seven to eight million dollars in developing the technology since the company was established in early 1995.
Currently, major televised sports events attract only large international advertisers, because they are the only ones who can afford such exposure.
If an event is broadcast to 80 countries, even large companies like Nike and Adidas might be interested in only 30 of those markets and would negotiate ad rates accordingly.
But with virtual advertising, the event owner could sell advertising for each market.
As a sports sponsor, Allied Domecq may even be able to make money by selling off advertising rights to local advertisers in markets in which the company lacks a strong interest.
"The money that comes in could potentially match the money you spend to buy the event," Burton said.
VIRTUAL ADVERTS STAGE THEIR DEBUT IN BRITAIN

Allied Domecq was first to use the technology in Britain when in mid-July it displayed virtual images of the logos of three of its brands on boards at each end of the pitch in a satellite television broadcast of the England versus Australia rugby game.
Allied Domecq used the EPSIS virtual advertising system developed by Syma Vision, a unit of France's Lagardhre Groupe.
"I think this technology is going to change the world of sports advertising," Burton told Reuters.
EPSIS is one of the three virtual advertising systems developed around the world. The other two have been developed by Israel-based SciTex and U.S.-based Princeton Video Imaging.
GETTING AROUND ADVERTISING BANS
Virtual advertising also offers the potential to advertise selectively products that are banned from television in some markets, such as tobacco and alcohol.

"When you get the French Grand Prix, Marlboro is not allowed to put on their cars the Marlboro name," Burton said. But with virtual advertising, "there's no reason why you couldn't put the Marlboro name on in every country where tobacco advertising is allowed".

The scheduled 1998 World Cup soccer championship in France, which also bans the advertising of alcoholic drinks, has led to speculation that advertisers such as sponsor Anheuser-Busch Cos Inc might find virtual advertising the answer to their problems.
Anheuser-Busch, the maker of Budweiser beer, had been striving earlier this year to find a way round the rule.
"It would be perfectly possible for Budweiser to get around its problem in France with the World Cup," said ISG's Impey. "You could show Budweiser in the UK and have Pepsi in France."
